dossier.public_summary: The dip does not come from the target star; TESS difference images locate it about 26 arcseconds away at high significance, the position of a nearby star that could produce the signal with a deep eclipse. With no on-target transit and neighbours able to mimic the dip, the best explanation is a background/blended eclipsing binary, not a planet around the target.

reasons.why: Difference imaging puts the dip 26.2" from the target at 16.7 sigma, inconsistent with the target. This is positive evidence the signal is on a neighbour, not a planet transiting the target.
All-sector centroid confirms off-target with same 26.2" offset; high diff_snr 66.23.

Two stars within one pixel can plausibly cause the 1946 ppm dip with <=25% eclipse, and 33 more within the aperture can with deeper eclipses, including one at 16.2" needing 12.98%, consistent with centroid offset.

Secondary near 0.62 phase at 0.44 x dip depth is suggestive of a stellar companion, though below 5 sigma formal threshold; with off-target centroid it favours a blended eclipsing binary over a planet.
ML scorer trained on follow-up outcomes rates this as more false-positive (median planet 0.5, <0.1 rare for planets), consistent with off-target and similar signals which were not planets.
